## Quick questions, quick answers

The questions people ask most about this comparison, answered directly. Stats and pricing verified October 2026.

**Fireflies.ai vs Otter.ai — which free plan is better?**

Different trade-offs: Otter's free plan gives you 300 transcription minutes/month with a 30-minute conversation cap, plus the mobile app and in-person recording. Fireflies' free plan offers unlimited transcription with limited AI summaries and capped storage. Pick Fireflies if you want lots of raw transcripts; Otter if you need mobile or in-person meetings.

**Is Fireflies.ai or Otter.ai better for sales teams?**

Fireflies.ai, clearly. Talk ratios, sentiment tracking, and notes pushed automatically into HubSpot or Salesforce are built for sales calls feeding a CRM pipeline. Otter is the everyday-team-meetings tool — reliable transcription, a mobile app, and in-person recording. Buy for the call type: pipeline reviews favor Fireflies, general standups favor Otter.

**Which is cheaper: Fireflies.ai or Otter.ai?**

Otter Pro is $8.33/user/month billed annually ($16.99 month-to-month); Fireflies Pro is $10/user/month annual ($18 monthly). But model Fireflies' AI credit pool first — 20 AI credits/month on Pro, a one-time shared wallet on top of the subscription — because that's where Fireflies' real cost hides.

**Is Otter's mobile app actually a differentiator?**

Yes, if your meetings aren't always at a desk. Otter's mobile app and in-person recording are the main reason everyday teams pick it over Fireflies — Fireflies is built around joining virtual meetings with a notetaker bot, which doesn't help hallway conversations or on-site sessions.

## The quick verdict

Pick Otter.ai if you're a general team that needs reliable transcription, summaries, and search across everyday meetings — with a mobile app and in-person recording for hallway conversations. The free tier's 300 minutes/month is genuinely usable for light schedules.

Pick Fireflies.ai if your meetings are sales calls, and you need talk ratios, sentiment tracking, and notes pushed into HubSpot or Salesforce automatically. Unlimited transcription plus the CRM automation is the revenue-team stack.

The one-sentence version: Otter wins for general teams that want simple, metered transcription; Fireflies wins for sales teams that want meeting intelligence wired into their CRM.

The pricing philosophies differ as much as the products: Otter meters transcription minutes; Fireflies meters AI credits while transcription itself is unlimited. Both are per-user.

Two details that change the math. First, Fireflies' headline prices don't include AI usage: summaries, action items, and AskFred consume AI credits (20/month on Pro, 30/month on Business), and heavy AI users buy top-ups. 2026 pricing analyses flag this as the most under-discussed cost in the category. Second, Otter's free tier caps conversations at 30 minutes — a normal hour-long meeting gets cut off, which makes the free plan a trial for real teams rather than a permanent solution.

## Fireflies' credit system, explained

This deserves its own section because it's the #1 source of billing surprise. On every Fireflies plan — including paid ones — advanced AI features (AI summaries beyond the allowance, AskFred queries, Smart Highlights, custom AI skills) consume AI credits from a monthly pool. Pro gets 20/month, Business 30/month. Transcription itself is unlimited; the credits govern the intelligence layer on top.

For a salesperson who asks Fred to summarize every call and pull action items, 20–30 credits can run out before month-end. Top-ups are available, but they turn a $19/user/month line item into a variable one. If your team will lean hard on AI summaries, model this before committing — or compare against Otter's fixed minute allowance, which at least fails loudly and predictably when you hit it.

## Feature comparison

Three differences settle it: Fireflies.ai has conversation intelligence (talk ratios, sentiment, competitor mentions) and 100+ CRM integrations, while Otter.ai has live real-time captions and a mobile app with in-person recording. Otter offers file imports within its minute caps; Fireflies records video on paid tiers but Otter doesn't. The decider: CRM pipeline buyers take Fireflies, meeting-heavy mobile users take Otter.

## Meeting intelligence vs transcription

Fireflies' edge — and it's the reason sales teams pick it. Beyond transcription, Fireflies analyzes how the meeting went: who talked how much, whether sentiment shifted, when competitors got mentioned, which topics consumed the most time. For a sales manager coaching five reps, that's a performance dataset, not a notes tool. The workflow automation completes the picture — notes, tasks, and CRM updates happen without anyone opening HubSpot. Reviewers consistently describe the setup as heavier than Otter's, but the payoff lands for teams where calls are revenue.

Otter's edge — and why general teams default to it. Otter is the simpler, broader tool: live transcription you can watch during the call, a genuinely good mobile app, and in-person recording that covers conference rooms and hallway conversations no bot can join. It's the meeting assistant for the whole company, not just the sales floor. The trade-offs are the minute meters — 300 minutes on free, 1,200 on Pro — and the absence of Fireflies' analytics layer. If your heaviest meeting user is in product or operations, not sales, those meters are the more honest constraint.

## Who should pick Fireflies.ai, and who should pick Otter.ai?

Pick Otter.ai for everyday team meetings: 300 free minutes a month, reliable transcription, a mobile app, and in-person recording. Pick Fireflies.ai for sales calls: unlimited transcription with talk ratios, sentiment tracking, and notes pushed into HubSpot or Salesforce automatically. Fireflies runs $10–$18/user/month on annual billing.

### Pick Fireflies.ai if…

- Your meetings are sales calls and revenue conversations

- You live in HubSpot or Salesforce

- You want talk-time, sentiment, and topic analytics

- Unlimited transcription matters more than fixed minutes

- You need 100+ integrations and workflow automation

### Pick Otter.ai if…

- You're a general team with everyday meetings

- You need a mobile app or in-person recording

- You want live transcription during the call

- You prefer fixed minute limits over credit systems

- You want the simplest setup in the category

## Quick answers

### Is Fireflies or Otter cheaper for heavy meeting loads?

Fireflies is cheaper once you record a lot. Otter meters transcription minutes (Pro caps at 1,200/month; $16.99/user monthly or $8.33 annual), while Fireflies Pro is $18 monthly or $10 annual with unlimited transcription. Past ~20 recorded hours a month, Fireflies wins; lighter users pay less with Otter. Note Fireflies AI credits are a separate monthly pool (20 on Pro, 30 on Business).

### Which is better for sales teams — Fireflies or Otter?

Fireflies. It tracks talk ratios, sentiment shifts, and competitor mentions, and pushes notes and tasks into HubSpot or Salesforce automatically — a sales-coaching dataset, not just notes. Otter is built for everyday transcription: a mobile app, in-person recording, and live captions, with no sales-intelligence layer.

### Does Fireflies' free plan beat Otter's?

For raw volume, yes. Fireflies' free tier includes unlimited transcription (with limited AI summaries and storage); Otter's free tier gives 300 minutes a month with 30-minute conversation caps. Occasional recorders are fine on Otter free; heavy recorders who don't need full AI features get more from Fireflies free.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Fireflies.ai really unlimited?**

Transcription is unlimited on all plans, but the AI layer isn't: summaries, AskFred, and smart highlights consume monthly AI credits (20 on Pro, 30 on Business), and storage is metered on Free and Pro. It's unlimited recording, metered intelligence — budget the AI credits against how many summaries you'll actually read.

**Can I use Otter.ai free forever?**

For light use, yes — 300 minutes/month with real-time transcription is genuinely usable. But the 30-minute conversation cap cuts off normal hour-long meetings, and file imports are limited to 3 lifetime on the free plan. Heavy users land on Pro ($16.99/month) fast.

**Do attendees know they're being recorded?**

Yes — both join as visible bots (Fireflies as "Fireflies.ai Notetaker," Otter as OtterPilot) and announce themselves. Recording consent laws vary by jurisdiction: disclose recording at the start of every call regardless, and check your company's policy before enabling auto-join.

**Which integrates better with Salesforce?**

Fireflies — it's the deeper integration, with automatic note and task pushing plus conversation intelligence mapped to deal records. Otter offers Salesforce and HubSpot connectors on Pro and up, but the automation depth is shallower. If Salesforce is where your deals live, Fireflies' automatic syncing saves your reps the manual logging Otter still requires.

**What happens when I run out of Fireflies AI credits?**

Transcription and recording continue — only AI features (summaries, AskFred, smart highlights) pause until credits reset or you buy top-ups. It's a softer failure than hitting Otter's minute cap, but it can still leave a sales team without summaries mid-month.

**Which is better for non-sales teams?**

Otter.ai. Product, operations, and leadership meetings need reliable transcription and search, not talk-ratio analytics — and Otter's mobile app plus in-person recording cover meetings that Fireflies' bot model can't reach. Sales teams get more from Fireflies' coaching metrics; everyone else should default to Otter.

**Fireflies.ai vs Otter.ai — which free plan is better?**

Different trade-offs: Otter's free plan gives you 300 transcription minutes/month with a 30-minute conversation cap, plus the mobile app and in-person recording. Fireflies' free plan offers unlimited transcription with limited AI summaries and capped storage. Pick Fireflies if you want lots of raw transcripts; Otter if you need mobile or in-person meetings.

**Is Fireflies.ai or Otter.ai better for sales teams?**

Fireflies.ai, clearly. Talk ratios, sentiment tracking, and notes pushed automatically into HubSpot or Salesforce are built for sales calls feeding a CRM pipeline. Otter is the everyday-team-meetings tool — reliable transcription, a mobile app, and in-person recording. Buy for the call type: pipeline reviews favor Fireflies, general standups favor Otter.

**Which is cheaper: Fireflies.ai or Otter.ai?**

Otter Pro is $8.33/user/month billed annually ($16.99 month-to-month); Fireflies Pro is $10/user/month annual ($18 monthly). But model Fireflies' AI credit pool first — 20 AI credits/month on Pro, a one-time shared wallet on top of the subscription — because that's where Fireflies' real cost hides.

**Is Otter's mobile app actually a differentiator?**

Yes, if your meetings aren't always at a desk. Otter's mobile app and in-person recording are the main reason everyday teams pick it over Fireflies — Fireflies is built around joining virtual meetings with a notetaker bot, which doesn't help hallway conversations or on-site sessions. Fully remote teams should compare the tools on other grounds instead.

**Is Fireflies or Otter better for podcasters?**

For remote guest interviews, Fireflies: unlimited transcription on the free plan means long sessions don't burn a minute budget — though AI summaries and storage are limited on free. Otter's free plan caps at 300 minutes/month with a 30-minute conversation cap, which cuts off hour-long episodes. For in-studio recording, Otter's app and in-person capture win instead.

**Which is better for recruiting and screening calls?**

Fireflies. High-volume screening is a pipeline problem: unlimited transcription plus talk ratios, sentiment tracking, and notes pushed into HubSpot or Salesforce via 100+ integrations. Fireflies Pro is $18/user/month ($10 annual). Otter ($16.99/mo, $8.33 annual) is the simpler pick when you only need reliable transcription and a mobile app.

**Do Fireflies.ai and Otter.ai work with Microsoft Teams?**

Yes — both join your Zoom, Meet, and Teams calls, transcribe everything, and hand you AI summaries. Fireflies joins as its 'Fred' notetaker bot and Otter as OtterPilot, both via calendar auto-join. Platform coverage isn't the differentiator here — pick on sales intelligence (Fireflies) versus mobile and in-person recording (Otter).

**Can I upload audio or video files to Fireflies or Otter?**

Both, with different caps. Fireflies supports file imports on the paid tiers, but they're storage-metered. Otter's limits are explicit: 3 lifetime imports on free, 10 per month on Pro, and unlimited on Business. Heavy uploaders should note Otter meters transcription minutes — uploads land inside the 300 free minutes/month — while Fireflies' transcription is unlimited.

**Is Fireflies or Otter more accurate?**

The page doesn't declare a hands-on accuracy winner — verdicts come from pricing analysis, documented feature lists, and aggregated reviews, not lab tests. Both are treated as reliable transcription. The real differences: Otter's live real-time captions for watching the call as it happens, and Fireflies' post-meeting intelligence — talk ratios, sentiment, competitor mentions.

## Final verdict

Worth it for sales teams: Fireflies.ai. Unlimited transcription, conversation intelligence, and CRM automation at $10–$18/user/month (annual) is a purpose-built revenue stack. Just model the AI credit pool honestly before committing — the headline price isn't the whole price for heavy AI users.

Worth it for general teams: Otter.ai. The default pick for everyone else: live transcription, a real mobile app, in-person recording, and pricing that scales from a usable free tier to $8.33–$19.99/user/month. Simple, predictable, and the easiest setup in the category.

Skip Fireflies if your meetings aren't sales calls — you'll pay for intelligence features you never open. Skip Otter if your pipeline depends on call analytics and CRM automation — minute meters don't coach reps.

### Ready to decide?

Both have genuinely usable free tiers — run your next week of meetings on both and let the workflow decide.

## GetResponse vs Mailchimp: The Honest 2026 Breakdown
URL: https://worthitstack.com/getresponse-vs-mailchimp.html · Last updated (as shown on page): October 2026

# GetResponse vs Mailchimp: The Honest 2026 Breakdown

Last updated October 2026 · 9 min read · Pricing verified September 2026

In short: Pick GetResponse if your list is going to grow — deeper automation per dollar, gentler per-contact pricing as contacts increase, and webinars bundled into the same tool. Pick Mailchimp if you want the easiest possible start, the prettiest templates, and the Intuit ecosystem. Growing lists should lean GetResponse; beginners should lean Mailchimp. Confirm current pricing before buying.

GetResponse and Mailchimp are the two names that come up in almost every "which email tool?" conversation — and they represent two genuinely different philosophies. Mailchimp is the friendly giant: famously easy to start, beautifully designed, now part of Intuit. GetResponse is the veteran workhorse: around since the late 1990s, deeper automation at lower prices, and a habit of bundling extras (like webinars) that competitors charge separately for.

Most comparisons declare a single winner and move on. We won't do that, because the honest answer depends on your list size, your budget, and how much automation you actually need. Here's the full breakdown.

## Stats worth citing

Current numbers from this comparison's at-a-glance table, sourced from each tool's official pricing page — quote them with the link. Stats verified October 2026.

- Entry paid: GetResponse Email Marketing from $19/mo (1,000 contacts) vs Mailchimp Essentials from $13/mo (500 contacts) — Mailchimp is cheaper to start, GetResponse prices contacts more gently as the list grows. Source: GetResponse official pricing (https://www.getresponse.com/pricing) · Source: Mailchimp official pricing (https://mailchimp.com/pricing)

- Both free plans cover up to 500 contacts — but Mailchimp free caps at 1,000 sends/month with Mailchimp branding, while GetResponse free goes up to 500 contacts too. Source: GetResponse official pricing (https://www.getresponse.com/pricing) · Source: Mailchimp official pricing (https://mailchimp.com/pricing)

- Per-dollar differentiator: GetResponse bundles deeper automation plus webinars into the same tool; Mailchimp trades automation depth for templates and Intuit-ecosystem ease. Source: GetResponse official pricing (https://www.getresponse.com/pricing) · Source: Mailchimp official pricing (https://mailchimp.com/pricing)

## GetResponse vs Mailchimp at a glance

Growing lists should lean GetResponse ($19/month from 1,000 contacts) — deeper automation per dollar, gentler per-contact pricing as you scale, and webinars bundled in. Beginners should lean Mailchimp (Essentials from $13/month for 500 contacts) — the easiest start and prettiest templates, with Intuit Assist for subject lines. Both offer free plans up to 500 contacts. Confirm current pricing before buying.

|  | GetResponse | Mailchimp |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting price | Email Marketing — from $19/mo (1,000 contacts) | Essentials — from $13/mo (500 contacts) |
| Free plan | Yes — $0 up to 500 contacts | Yes — $0 up to 500 contacts, 1,000 sends/month, Mailchimp branding |
| Automation per dollar | Deeper automation per dollar; webinars bundled into the same tool | Templates and Intuit-ecosystem ease over automation depth |
| Best for | Growing lists — gentler per-contact pricing as contacts increase | Beginners — easiest start, prettiest templates |
| Pick it if | Your list is going to grow | You want the easiest possible start |
| Our one-line bottom line | Growing lists should lean GetResponse; beginners should lean Mailchimp. Confirm current pricing before buying. |  |

## Quick questions, quick answers

The questions people ask most about this comparison, answered directly. Stats and pricing verified October 2026.

**GetResponse vs Mailchimp — which is cheaper as my list grows?**

GetResponse gets relatively cheaper: its Email Marketing plan starts from $19/month for 1,000 contacts with gentler per-contact pricing as you grow. Mailchimp Essentials starts from $13/month for 500 contacts but its contact-based scaling is steeper. Beginners save on Mailchimp; growing lists save on GetResponse.

**Which has better automation: GetResponse or Mailchimp?**

GetResponse — deeper automation per dollar, with webinars bundled into the same tool. Mailchimp wins on templates, ease of use, and the Intuit ecosystem, but automation depth is GetResponse's territory.

**Is GetResponse or Mailchimp better for a complete beginner?**

Mailchimp — the easiest start, prettiest templates, and the Intuit ecosystem make it the friendliest onboarding. The caveat: if you're a beginner who plans to grow a list, GetResponse's $0-for-500-contacts free plan plus its webinar bundle may be the cheaper long-term home.

**Does GetResponse really include webinars?**

Yes — webinars are bundled into the same GetResponse tool rather than sold as a separate product. That's one of its clearest edges over Mailchimp at comparable price points, especially for creators who run live or evergreen webinars and want email plus webinars on one bill.

## The quick verdict

Pick GetResponse if your list is going to grow, you want serious automation without paying premium-tier prices, or you'd like webinars bundled into the same tool. Its pricing scales more gently as your contacts increase.

Pick Mailchimp if you want the easiest possible start, care about design polish and templates, or live inside the Intuit ecosystem (QuickBooks, etc.). It's the smoother on-ramp — you just pay more as you scale.

The one-sentence version: GetResponse wins on value and automation depth; Mailchimp wins on simplicity and ecosystem. Growing lists should lean GetResponse.

## Pricing compared, tier by tier

Pricing is where this comparison gets interesting — and where most reviews mislead you by quoting only the cheapest tier. Both vendors charge by contact count and raise prices as your list grows, but they count very differently: Mailchimp bills in 500-contact blocks, GetResponse in 1,000-contact blocks. That structural difference matters more than the headline prices.

| Tier | GetResponse | Mailchimp |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free plan | $0 — up to 500 contacts, core email tools with limits | $0 — up to 500 contacts, 1,000 sends/month, Mailchimp branding |
| Entry paid | Email Marketing — from $19/mo (1,000 contacts) | Essentials — from $13/mo (500 contacts) |
| Mid paid | Marketing Automation — from $59/mo (1,000 contacts) | Standard — from $20/mo (500 contacts) |
| Top paid | Ecommerce Marketing — from $119/mo (1,000 contacts) | Premium — from $350/mo (500 contacts) |

Starting prices verified September 2026. Vendors change pricing often — confirm current pricing on the vendor's site before buying.

Here's the math that matters: at a small list, Mailchimp's entry point is genuinely cheaper ($13 vs $19). But as your list grows, Mailchimp's smaller billing blocks mean the per-contact cost climbs faster. A 5,000-contact list costs meaningfully more on Mailchimp than on GetResponse at comparable feature levels — run your own projected list size through both pricing calculators before deciding, because this is where the long-term winner is decided.

One more pricing note: Mailchimp's Premium tier at $350/mo is aimed at large senders with dedicated onboarding needs. Most small businesses will never need it — but its existence tells you where Mailchimp's pricing curve goes.

## Feature comparison

Three differences settle it: GetResponse bundles webinar hosting into upper plans and includes an ecommerce plan — Mailchimp has neither. Mailchimp counters with the smoother drag-and-drop builder, Intuit Assist AI, and 300+ integrations versus GetResponse's 170+. GetResponse goes deeper on automation per dollar; Mailchimp goes easier on first-time senders. Pick by list-growth plans, not the starting price.

| Feature | GetResponse | Mailchimp |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drag-and-drop email builder | Yes | Yes — widely considered the smoother builder |
| Visual automation workflows | Yes — deep branching from Marketing Automation ($59) | Yes — Customer Journey Builder on Standard ($20+), advanced branching costs more |
| AI email / subject-line generation | Yes — AI email generator | Yes — Intuit Assist (subject lines, send-time, creative help) |
| Landing pages | Yes — built-in builder | Yes — built-in builder |

| A/B testing | Yes | Yes (more variants on higher tiers) |
| Integrations | 170+ commonly cited | 300+ commonly cited — one of the largest ecosystems |
| Support | 24/7 chat on paid plans; email on free | Email/chat on paid plans; limited on free |

Feature availability verified against official documentation, September 2026. Vendors move features between tiers — confirm on the vendor's site.

## Ease of use

Mailchimp's edge — and it's a real one. Mailchimp practically invented friendly email software onboarding: the signup flow, the template picker, the plain-language guidance. If you've never sent a marketing email, you'll be sending one faster in Mailchimp. This is our assessment based on consistently reported user sentiment, not a lab test — but the pattern across reviews is unmistakable.

GetResponse isn't hard, exactly — it's just denser. More menus, more options, more power-user surface area. The trade-off is deliberate: that density is where the deeper automation lives. Beginners sometimes bounce off it; marketers who outgrow Mailchimp often land here.

## Automation depth

GetResponse's edge — the biggest gap in this comparison. GetResponse's visual workflow builder (available from the $59 Marketing Automation tier) supports genuinely complex branching: tag-based triggers, scoring, multi-path customer journeys. It's the kind of automation that usually costs much more elsewhere.

Mailchimp's Customer Journey Builder (Standard, from $20) is good for straightforward sequences — welcome series, abandoned carts, post-purchase follow-ups. But the more advanced branching and segmentation depth costs more, and power users consistently report hitting ceilings sooner. If automation is the reason you're buying an email tool, GetResponse gives you more of it per dollar.

## AI features

Both vendors now ship AI features, and both are worth a clear-eyed look rather than excitement:

- GetResponse: AI email generator (drafts full emails from a prompt), AI subject-line suggestions. Useful for beating blank-page syndrome.

- Mailchimp (Intuit Assist): AI-assisted subject lines and send-time optimization, plus creative assistant features that auto-generate branded designs.

The honest take: these are genuinely useful accelerators, not reasons to choose a platform. Nobody should pick an email tool because of its AI subject-line writer — pick it for automation depth, pricing at your scale, and deliverability, and treat the AI as a bonus. (Feature names and availability change often; verify what's current.)

## Webinars, landing pages & extras

Webinars are GetResponse's quiet superpower. Webinar hosting is bundled into its upper-tier plans — if you run webinars, this alone can replace a separate $50–100/mo webinar tool. No other major email platform in this price range does this. Mailchimp has nothing comparable; you'd integrate a third-party tool.

Both include landing page builders and signup forms that are perfectly serviceable for lead capture. Neither will replace a dedicated landing-page tool, but both mean you don't strictly need one to start.

## Deliverability & analytics

Both platforms operate dedicated deliverability infrastructure and offer the standard analytics suite: opens, clicks, bounces, unsubscribes, and A/B testing. Here's what we won't do: quote inbox-placement percentages as if they're stable facts. Independent deliverability tests vary by sender, list hygiene, and sending volume — your list hygiene matters more than which of these two you pick. Either platform, used well with a clean opt-in list, will land in inboxes fine.

## Who should pick GetResponse, and who should pick Mailchimp?

Pick GetResponse if your list is going to grow: deeper automation per dollar, gentler per-contact pricing as contacts scale, and webinars bundled in. Pick Mailchimp if you want the easiest start, the prettiest templates, and the Intuit ecosystem. Growing lists lean GetResponse; beginners lean Mailchimp.

### Pick GetResponse if…

- Your list is growing (or will) — the pricing math favors you

- You want deep automation without premium-tier prices

- You run webinars and want them in the same tool

- You're comfortable with a denser, more powerful interface

- You want funnels and landing pages bundled in

### Pick Mailchimp if…

- You want the easiest possible start — onboarding is unmatched

- Design polish and templates matter a lot to you

- You're in the Intuit ecosystem (QuickBooks etc.)

- Your list will stay small (under ~2,000 contacts)

- You want the largest integration marketplace

## Quick answers

### Is GetResponse cheaper than Mailchimp for growing lists?

Generally yes. GetResponse's Email Marketing tier starts around $19/month for 1,000 contacts, versus Mailchimp Essentials around $13/month for 500 — but Mailchimp's per-contact pricing climbs steeply as your list grows, while GetResponse scales more gently. Under ~2,000 contacts the gap is small; beyond that, GetResponse usually wins. Confirm current pricing before buying.

### Which is easier for a beginner — GetResponse or Mailchimp?

Mailchimp. Its onboarding is unmatched, its templates are the prettiest in the category, and the Intuit ecosystem is a real plus if you use QuickBooks. GetResponse trades some hand-holding for deeper automation per dollar. Beginners should lean Mailchimp; senders whose lists are about to grow should lean GetResponse.

### Does GetResponse include webinars?

Yes. Webinar hosting is bundled into GetResponse plans — unusual among email tools and a genuine part of its value case against Mailchimp, where you'd pay for a separate webinar platform. If you run webinars to grow your list, that single inclusion can swing the comparison on its own.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is GetResponse really cheaper than Mailchimp?**

At very small list sizes, no — Mailchimp's $13/mo Essentials undercuts GetResponse's $19/mo entry tier. The crossover happens as your list grows: Mailchimp bills in 500-contact blocks while GetResponse bills in 1,000-contact blocks, so GetResponse's per-contact cost scales more gently. Run your projected 12-month list size through both calculators.

**Does Mailchimp still have a free plan?**

Yes — Mailchimp's free plan covers up to 500 contacts and 1,000 sends per month, with Mailchimp branding on emails and limited features including limited support. It's genuinely usable for validating an idea before you pay anything; the paid tiers remove branding and unlock automation. Validate free, then upgrade only when sends or automation justify it.

**Which is better for a complete beginner?**

Mailchimp. Its onboarding flow, template library, and plain-language UI remain the easiest on-ramp in email marketing. GetResponse isn't difficult, but it assumes slightly more marketing familiarity. If you've never sent a campaign before, start with Mailchimp and only switch when you outgrow its automation or its pricing.

**Which has better marketing automation?**

GetResponse, by a clear margin at comparable prices. Its visual workflow builder (from the $59/month tier) supports deeper branching, contact scoring, and multi-path journeys than Mailchimp offers below its premium tiers. If automation is your main buying criterion, this category alone justifies the shortlist.

**Can I migrate my list from one to the other?**

Yes — both support CSV list imports, and both publish migration guides for switching platforms. Expect to rebuild automations and templates manually; there's no one-click migration of workflows between the two. Budget an afternoon for a small list with simple sequences, and longer when complex automations need rebuilding.

**Are the AI features worth paying for?**

Honestly? They're nice accelerators, not decision-drivers. AI subject lines and send-time optimization save time, but the core value of either platform is still automation depth, pricing at your scale, and your own list hygiene. Don't pick a platform for its AI writer.

**GetResponse vs Mailchimp — which is cheaper as my list grows?**

GetResponse gets relatively cheaper: its Email Marketing plan starts from $19/month for 1,000 contacts with gentler per-contact pricing as you grow. Mailchimp Essentials starts from $13/month for 500 contacts but its contact-based scaling is steeper. Beginners save on Mailchimp; growing lists save on GetResponse.

**Which has better automation: GetResponse or Mailchimp?**

GetResponse — deeper automation per dollar, with webinars bundled into the same tool. Mailchimp wins on templates, ease of use, and the Intuit ecosystem, but automation depth is GetResponse's territory. If automated sequences and funnels are the reason you're buying, GetResponse gives you more capability for the money.

**Is GetResponse or Mailchimp better for a complete beginner?**

Mailchimp — the easiest start, prettiest templates, and the Intuit ecosystem make it the friendliest onboarding. The caveat: if you're a beginner who plans to grow a list, GetResponse's $0-for-500-contacts free plan plus its webinar bundle may be the cheaper long-term home.

**Does GetResponse really include webinars?**

Yes — webinars are bundled into the same GetResponse tool rather than sold as a separate product. That's one of its clearest edges over Mailchimp at comparable price points, especially for creators who run live or evergreen webinars and want email plus webinars on one bill. Mailchimp buyers need a separate webinar tool.

**Which is better for a WordPress site: GetResponse or Mailchimp?**

Both work through WordPress plugins, so pick on pricing and depth. Mailchimp's 300+ integration ecosystem makes it the easier plug-in; GetResponse's 170+ integrations are fewer but deeper. The decider: Mailchimp Essentials starts at $13/month for 500 contacts but climbs steeply; GetResponse starts at $19/month for 1,000 with gentler per-contact scaling.

## Final verdict

For most small businesses with growth ambitions, GetResponse is the better buy — deeper automation per dollar, gentler pricing as your list scales, and bundled webinars that replace a separate subscription. For beginners who want the smoothest start, the prettiest templates, and the Intuit ecosystem, Mailchimp remains excellent — just go in eyes open about where its pricing curve goes.

Either way: start on a free plan, validate that email actually drives revenue for you, and only then commit to a paid tier at your real list size.

### Ready to decide?

Start free on either platform — upgrade only when your list earns it.

## GoHighLevel Review: Is It Really Worth It? (2026)
URL: https://worthitstack.com/gohighlevel-review.html · Last updated (as shown on page): October 2026

# GoHighLevel Review: Is It Really Worth It in 2026?

Last updated October 2026 · 10 min read · Pricing verified October 2026

In short: GoHighLevel is worth it for agencies and client-services businesses: the $297/month Unlimited plan replaces a $400–$600/month stack — CRM, funnels, email, SMS, calendar, courses, review management. Skip it solo with no clients, if you need a free plan (there isn't one), or want setup this week — the learning curve runs 2–4 weeks.

## Stats worth citing

Current numbers from this review’s at-a-glance table, sourced from the tool’s official pricing page — quote them with the link. Stats verified October 2026.

- $97/month (Starter); $297/month Unlimited is the value tier; up to $497/month — the $297 plan replaces a $400–$600/month stack (CRM, funnels, email, SMS, calendar, courses, review management), plus usage fees on top. Source: GoHighLevel official pricing (https://www.gohighlevel.com/pricing)

- No free plan exists at all — and reviewers report a 2–4 week learning curve, so don’t buy it if you need setup this week or you’re a solo operator with no clients. Source: GoHighLevel official pricing (https://www.gohighlevel.com/pricing)

- Agencies are the buyer: unlimited sub-accounts plus SaaS mode (resell at your own price); solo operators get the free plan and simpler setup at systeme.io instead. Source: GoHighLevel official pricing (https://www.gohighlevel.com/pricing)

GoHighLevel sells agencies a seductive promise: replace your CRM, funnel builder, email platform, SMS tool, calendar, course host, and review-management software with one flat subscription starting at $97/month. For an agency currently stitching together six tools at $400–$600/month, that's a serious pitch. The question this review answers: does the math survive contact with reality?

The short answer: for agencies and client-services businesses, yes — and it's not particularly close. The sub-account architecture is genuinely unmatched at this price, and the platform has kept its pricing stable for years while competitors kept raising theirs. But the headline price is never the whole bill, the learning curve is real, and solo operators are consistently oversold a platform they don't need. We also compared it head-to-head with its closest rival: GoHighLevel vs systeme.io .

A note on how we work: our verdicts come from pricing analysis, documented feature lists, and aggregated verified reviews — not hands-on lab tests. When review sentiment is consistent across sources, we say so; when sources conflict, we say that too.

## GoHighLevel at a glance

GoHighLevel is the best agency-infrastructure value in marketing software at $97/month Starter (up to $497/month), with sub-accounts, white-labeling, and CRM depth nothing else matches. There's no free plan, a genuinely steep 2–4 week learning curve, and $20–$150/month metered usage fees on top of every plan. Solo operators with no clients should start with systeme.io's free plan instead.

| Starting price | $97/month (Starter); $297/month Unlimited is the value tier; up to $497/month |
| --- | --- |
| Free plan | No — there is no free plan |
| Best for | Agencies and client-services businesses — the $297 plan replaces a $400–$600/month stack |
| Skip if | You’re a solo operator with no clients, want a free plan, or need setup this week (2–4 week learning curve) |
| Top alternative | — free plan and simpler setup for solo operators |

## Quick questions, quick answers

The questions people ask most about this tool, answered directly. Stats and pricing verified October 2026.

**Is GoHighLevel worth it for a solo business?**

Usually not. There's no free plan, reviewers report a 2–4 week learning curve, and it's built for agencies and client-services businesses. Solo operators are better served by systeme.io — free plan, simpler setup — unless you plan to take on clients soon.

**Does GoHighLevel have a free plan or free trial?**

No free plan. Starter is $97/month, Unlimited $297/month (the value tier), up to $497/month — and metered usage ($20–$150/mo for calls, SMS, email, AI) sits on top. Budget the usage line item, not just the plan.

**What does GoHighLevel actually replace?**

For the $297/month Unlimited plan: CRM, funnels, email, SMS, calendar, courses, and review management — a $400–$600/month stack consolidated into one subscription. Add flat unlimited contacts at every tier with no per-contact tax, and the agency pitch is clear.

**GoHighLevel vs systeme.io — which is cheaper?**

systeme.io by a mile: free for 2,000 contacts, paid from $17/month, caps at $97/month. GoHighLevel starts at $97/month with usage fees on top and no free plan. But they're different buyers — systeme.io for solo digital-product businesses, GoHighLevel for agencies that can resell the platform.

## What's the quick verdict on GoHighLevel?

Worth it if you run an agency, manage 2+ clients, or need a real CRM with pipelines, two-way SMS, and automated follow-up — the $297/month Unlimited plan replaces a $400–$600/month stack of separate tools and the per-client cost drops fast as you grow.

Skip it if you're one person with one offer and no clients (you'll pay agency prices for agency capacity you'll never use), you want a free plan (there isn't one), or you need a simple setup this week — reviewers consistently report a 2–4 week learning curve.

The one-sentence version: GoHighLevel is the best agency-infrastructure value in marketing software at $97–$497/month, with the catches fully visible: usage fees on top of the base price, a genuinely steep learning curve, and zero reason to exist for simple solo setups.

## Pricing: the three tiers, honestly

GoHighLevel's pricing has barely moved in years — while competitors crept upward, the core Starter and Unlimited prices stayed put, which 2026 pricing analyses consistently flag as remarkable. The structure is clean: all three tiers include the same core features (unlimited contacts, unlimited users, full CRM, funnel builder, workflow automation, email + SMS marketing, booking calendar, reputation management, course hosting, 24/7 support). What changes is sub-account capacity, white-labeling, and the resale layer — not feature access.

| Tier | Monthly | Annual (effective) | Sub-accounts | What it adds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Starter | $97/mo | $970/yr (~$81/mo) | 3 | Full platform access for your own business. No white-labeling, no usage rebilling — a tool for your business, not a business in itself. |
| Unlimited | $297/mo | $2,970/yr (~$248/mo) | Unlimited | The agency tier: unlimited client sub-accounts, white-label desktop, usage rebilling at cost, basic API access. Most popular tier per 2026 breakdowns. |
| Agency Pro | $497/mo | $4,970/yr (~$414/mo) | Unlimited | Adds SaaS Mode: resell the platform under your own brand, automated sub-account creation, mark up usage up to 10x, white-label mobile app, advanced API. |

Pricing verified October 2026 against GoHighLevel's published pricing and multiple 2026 pricing breakdowns. Annual billing saves roughly two months (~16–17%): $194/yr on Starter, $594/yr on Unlimited, ~$994/yr on Agency Pro. Monthly billing has no long-term contract — upgrade, downgrade, or cancel from the dashboard. Every tier starts with a 14-day trial (a 30-day trial is available via the bootcamp promo, per 2026 reviews). There is no free plan.

## The real bill: usage fees

The base plan is never the whole bill. SMS, voice calls, email volume, phone numbers, and AI features are metered on top. 2026 pricing analyses consistently put typical usage at an extra $20–$150/month depending on volume — budget it from day one, not as a surprise. A solo operator on Starter with moderate SMS and the AI add-on typically lands around $150–$300/month all-in once usage settles, per independent 2026 cost breakdowns.

The line items worth knowing before you sign:

- AI Employee: $50/month per sub-account (Growth: 1,000 conversation responses + 100 voice minutes) or $97/month per sub-account for unlimited — not included in any base plan.

- Voice AI pay-per-use: roughly $0.06–$0.08 per minute on consumption pricing.

- Carrier fees: SMS/voice carrier surcharges increased in 2026 (AT&T from April, Verizon from May) — another small line item that flows through to your bill or your clients'.

- Extras on the meter: dedicated email IP (~$59/month), WhatsApp (~$10/month per sub-account), white-label mobile app ($497/month), HIPAA compliance ($297/month).

Here's the fair framing: Unlimited and Agency Pro let you rebill phone and email usage to clients (Unlimited at cost; Agency Pro with markup). At three clients paying even modest retainers, the platform cost per client drops under $100/month before usage — and the stack it replaces (funnels + email tool + Calendly + SMS + reputation management) is priced at $400–$600/month separately in 2026 reviews. The fee structure hurts solo users and rewards agencies, which is exactly the intended design.

## What it actually does

The CRM is the product's heart, and it's a real one. Visual pipelines, opportunity tracking, custom fields, tags, and smart lists — with clean separation between client sub-accounts. The workflow builder runs multi-channel automations across email, SMS, voice calls, and WhatsApp, with missed-call text-back and automated review requests baked in. For an agency running follow-up for ten local businesses, this combination is the reason the platform exists.

The supporting cast is genuinely full: 1,000+ funnel and landing page templates commonly cited, email campaigns plus multi-channel automation, a booking calendar with reminders, course and membership hosting, and a reputation module that requests and tracks Google reviews in-platform. The SaaS Mode on Agency Pro is the headline differentiator — white-label the whole platform under your brand, spin up sub-accounts automatically, and charge your own clients their own price for it. 2026 pricing analyses put SaaS Mode's break-even around two clients paying ~$297/month each. That's a business model, not a feature.

One structural note: the three tiers share the same core features — the difference is sub-account limits, white-labeling depth, and resale economics. Starter's three sub-accounts are enough for most solo setups (main business, a testing account, one spare), but the ceiling hits fast once you manage more than two active clients.

## The three catches

1. The learning curve is genuinely steep. This is the most consistent theme in 2026 review sentiment — reviewers describe a busy first two to four weeks: workflow builder, sub-account setup, phone and email configuration all take real learning. The platform scores well (~4.6/5 on G2 in 2026 roundups, lower on Capterra), but the praise comes overwhelmingly from agencies who invested the time. If you want "simple," this isn't it — it's "powerful," and powerful takes onboarding.

2. The headline price is never the whole bill. Covered above — but it bears repeating as a catch, because the "$97/month replaces everything" pitch lands differently when your second month's invoice shows usage lines you didn't budget. Go in knowing the real all-in number, or the platform will feel like it misled you. It didn't — the meter is documented — but it does require reading.

3. Solo businesses are consistently oversold. A solo creator with one offer doesn't need sub-accounts, white-labeling, rebilling, or SaaS mode — but pays for the infrastructure anyway on every tier above what they'd otherwise buy. There's no free plan to soften the landing, and the usage-meter economics only help once client revenue covers the base. For one funnel plus a mailing list, the value equation usually loses to cheaper all-in-ones.

A fourth, quieter theme in reviews: occasional bugginess. Complaints cluster here when they exist — the platform ships features fast and sometimes rough. It's the trade you accept for a platform that moves this quickly at this price.

## Who should buy it

### Worth it if…

- You run an agency or manage 2+ clients

- You need pipelines, deal tracking, and SMS follow-up

- You want to white-label or resell software as a service

- You're replacing a $400+/month stack of separate tools

- You can invest 2–4 weeks in learning the platform

### Skip it if…

- You're one person with one offer and no clients

- You want a free plan or a cheap entry point

- You need to be live this week, not next month

- SMS, pipelines, and multi-client work are irrelevant to you

- Metered usage fees would stress you out

## How it compares to alternatives

vs systeme.io: the classic ladder question. Systeme.io ($0–$97/month) is the solo-operator play — funnels, email, courses, and affiliate management for one business, free to start. GoHighLevel ($97–$497/month) is the agency play — CRM depth, sub-accounts, SMS, white-labeling. The honest path: start on systeme.io free, graduate to GoHighLevel when client #2 or #3 arrives. Full head-to-head breakdown .

vs HubSpot: structural mismatch. HubSpot is per-seat CRM depth and reporting for one company's book of business; GoHighLevel is flat-rate multi-client infrastructure you can resell. Agencies running 20 sub-accounts on the $297/month plan pay roughly $15/client/month before usage — a number HubSpot's per-seat model was never built to hit.

vs Kajabi / ClickFunnels / Kartra: these are creator and funnel-first platforms, not agency CRM. Kajabi wins on course-brand experience, ClickFunnels on funnel templates, but neither does sub-accounts, white-label resale, or native SMS follow-up at this price. Different product category wearing similar marketing.

## Frequently asked questions

**How much does GoHighLevel cost in 2026?**

Three tiers: Starter at $97/month, Unlimited at $297/month, and Agency Pro at $497/month. Annual billing drops the effective rate to about $81, $248, and $414/month respectively. Budget an extra $20–$150/month in usage fees for SMS, calls, email volume, and AI features on top of the base price.

**Does GoHighLevel have a free plan?**

No — there is no free plan. Every tier starts with a 14-day free trial, and a 30-day trial is available through HighLevel's bootcamp promo according to 2026 reviews. The $97/month entry price is deliberate: it's built for businesses and agencies, not hobbyists.

**What's the catch with GoHighLevel?**

Three honest ones: the learning curve is steep (2–4 weeks to get comfortable, per reviewers), the headline price is never the whole bill (usage fees for SMS, calls, email, and AI stack on top), and solo operators pay for agency capacity they may never use. Occasional bugginess shows up in reviews too.

**Is GoHighLevel good for a solo business?**

It works on the $97/month Starter plan, but it's often the wrong value equation for one offer and no clients — you're paying for sub-accounts, white-labeling, and rebilling infrastructure you won't touch. Solo businesses with one funnel and a mailing list are usually cheaper and simpler on platforms like systeme.io.

**Can you resell GoHighLevel to clients?**

Yes — that's the platform's signature move. The $497/month Agency Pro tier adds SaaS Mode: white-label the platform under your own brand, spin up sub-accounts automatically, and mark up usage fees to clients. 2026 pricing analyses put SaaS Mode's break-even around two clients paying ~$297/month each.

**Does GoHighLevel have an affiliate program?**

Yes — and it's one of the most lucrative in the agency-software space: 40% recurring commission on every referred plan. At $97–$497/month per customer, that's roughly $39–$119/month per referral for as long as they stay, which is why so much of the internet's GoHighLevel coverage is affiliate-driven.

**Is GoHighLevel worth it for a solo business?**

Usually not. There's no free plan, reviewers report a 2–4 week learning curve, and it's built for agencies and client-services businesses. Solo operators are better served by systeme.io — free plan, simpler setup — unless you plan to take on clients soon.

**Does GoHighLevel have a free plan or free trial?**

No free plan. Starter is $97/month, Unlimited $297/month (the value tier), up to $497/month — and metered usage ($20–$150/mo for calls, SMS, email, AI) sits on top. Budget the usage line item, not just the plan. Plan for a paid start; there is no free tier to grow into it from.

**What does GoHighLevel actually replace?**

For the $297/month Unlimited plan: CRM, funnels, email, SMS, calendar, courses, and review management — a $400–$600/month stack consolidated into one subscription. Add flat unlimited contacts at every tier with no per-contact tax, and the agency pitch is clear. That consolidation is the entire value case for the Unlimited tier.

**GoHighLevel vs systeme.io — which is cheaper?**

systeme.io by a mile: free for 2,000 contacts, paid from $17/month, caps at $97/month. GoHighLevel starts at $97/month with usage fees on top and no free plan. But they're different buyers — systeme.io for solo digital-product businesses, GoHighLevel for agencies that can resell the platform.

## Final verdict

Worth it if you sell to clients: GoHighLevel. The $97 Starter plan is a reasonable learning tier; the $297 Unlimited plan is where the business model clicks — per-client costs drop fast as you add accounts, and it replaces a $400–$600/month stack of separate tools. Just go in eyes open about the 2–4 week learning curve and the usage fees on top of the base price.

Skip it if you're solo. One person, one offer, no clients — you'll pay agency prices for agency capacity you'll never use, with no free plan to soften the landing. The cheaper all-in-ones exist for a reason, and plenty of businesses start there and graduate to GoHighLevel when client revenue covers the bill.

And the macro point: the pricing hasn't moved in years while competitors raised theirs, the affiliate terms (40% recurring) are among the best in SaaS, and the SaaS Mode break-even math is real. This is a platform built by people who understand the agency business model — buy it if you're in that business.

### Running an agency?

Start the 14-day trial and audit your current stack — if you're paying $400+/month across separate tools, the math usually speaks for itself.

## GoHighLevel vs Keap: Which CRM Wins in 2026?

# GoHighLevel vs Keap: Which CRM Wins in 2026?

Last updated October 2026 · 11 min read · Pricing verified October 2026

In short: Pick GoHighLevel if you run an agency — its sub-account and SaaS model has no rival — or want flat unlimited-contact billing starting at $97/month. Pick Keap if you're a small business with a modest list where the contact tax doesn't bite, $129–$229/month. Agencies shouldn't compare these — Keap has no agency model.

On paper they're the same pitch: one subscription that replaces your CRM, email tool, funnel builder, and appointment scheduler. In practice they're built for opposite buyers. Keap (the company formerly known as Infusionsoft) is the small-business automation veteran — the deepest campaign builder in this price class, billing you per contact. GoHighLevel is the agency disruptor — flat pricing with unlimited contacts and a sub-account model that lets agencies run dozens of clients on one bill.

The entire comparison reduces to one structural difference: Keap's bill grows with your list; GoHighLevel's doesn't. Everything else — features, moats, catches — flows from that. Here's the contact-tax math, the feature comparison, and the honest verdict.

A note on how we work: our verdicts come from pricing analysis, documented feature lists, and aggregated verified reviews — not hands-on lab tests. One caution for your own research: Keap has restructured its plans repeatedly (Lite/Pro/Max, Pro/Max Classic, contact-tier bands), and published 2026 figures vary by source. Treat every dollar figure below as the most commonly published 2026 rate and confirm on each vendor's pricing page before buying.

## Stats worth citing

- Entry math: GoHighLevel Starter from $97/mo ($970/yr) with unlimited contacts vs Keap Pro-tier ~$129–$229/mo capped at 1,500 contacts — Keap costs more at entry and still rations the list. Source: GoHighLevel official pricing (https://www.gohighlevel.com/pricing) · Source: Keap official pricing (https://keap.com/pricing)

- Contact-billing flip: GoHighLevel bills flat unlimited contacts at every tier (only metered usage varies, $20–$150/mo for calls, SMS, email, AI); Keap applies contact-tier step-ups as the list grows past 1,500 contacts, plus ~$29–$30/mo per extra user — a growing list punishes Keap’s pricing and barely touches GoHighLevel’s. Source: GoHighLevel official pricing (https://www.gohighlevel.com/pricing) · Source: Keap official pricing (https://keap.com/pricing)

- Agency model: GoHighLevel offers unlimited sub-accounts plus SaaS mode (resell at your own price); Keap has no agency model at all — agencies shouldn’t compare these on price, Keap fails the qualifier. Source: GoHighLevel official pricing (https://www.gohighlevel.com/pricing) · Source: Keap official pricing (https://keap.com/pricing)

## GoHighLevel vs Keap at a glance

Agencies shouldn't compare these at all — Keap has no agency model, so pick GoHighLevel ($97/month flat, unlimited contacts, sub-accounts, SaaS resale) for client work. Keap (~$129–$229/month, 1,500 contacts) is for small businesses that live inside automation. The billing quirks decide the rest: GoHighLevel adds $20–$150/month metered usage on top, while Keap steps contact tiers up as your list grows.

## Quick questions, quick answers

The questions people ask most about this comparison, answered directly. Stats and pricing verified October 2026.

**GoHighLevel vs Keap — which is better?**

For agencies, GoHighLevel — no contest: unlimited sub-accounts, SaaS mode, and white-label resale that Keap simply doesn't have. For a small business that lives inside automation with a modest list, Keap's automation moat can justify its ~$129–$229/mo Pro-tier pricing (1,500 contacts) — as long as the contact tax doesn't bite.

**How much does GoHighLevel really cost per month?**

Starter is $97/mo ($970/yr) with unlimited contacts, Unlimited $297/mo, Agency Pro $497/mo — and then metered usage on top: $20–$150/mo for calls, SMS, email, and AI depending on volume. Budget the usage line item, not just the plan.

**What happens to my bill as my contact list grows on each?**

This is the deciding math. GoHighLevel: flat unlimited contacts at every tier — the only variable is metered usage ($20–$150/mo for calls, SMS, email, AI). Keap: contact-tier step-ups as your list grows past 1,500 contacts, plus ~$29–$30/mo per extra user. A growing list punishes Keap's pricing and barely touches GoHighLevel's.

**Why do agencies pick GoHighLevel over Keap?**

The agency model: unlimited sub-accounts, SaaS mode that lets you resell the platform at your own price, and white-labeling — none of which Keap has. Add flat unlimited-contact billing and it's not a real contest for agency workflows. Keap's play is the automation moat for small businesses, not agencies.

## The quick verdict

Pick GoHighLevel if you run an agency (the sub-account + SaaS model has no rival), want flat unlimited-contact billing, or need funnels, websites, and a phone system in one bill. Entry: $97/month flat, unlimited contacts.

Pick Keap if you're a single small business that lives inside automation — its campaign builder is the deepest in the class — and your list is modest enough that the contact tax doesn't bite. Entry: roughly $129–$229/month at published 2026 rates, contact-limited.

The honest split: agencies shouldn't be comparing these two at all — Keap has no agency model. And solo operators should price year one with their actual list size, not the sticker price.

## Pricing compared, tier by tier

GoHighLevel's pricing is simple: three tiers, flat, unlimited contacts on all of them. Keap's is contact-based, and the 2026 numbers vary by source because Keap keeps restructuring — here's the most commonly published picture, verified October 2026.

| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry | Starter $97/mo ($970/yr) — CRM, funnels, websites, email/SMS marketing, calendar, workflows, unlimited contacts, 1 account | Pro-tier ~$129–$229/mo — 1,500 contacts, 1–2 users, CRM + email, automation, appointments, landing pages, sales pipelines, Keap Pay |
| Mid | Unlimited $297/mo ($2,970/yr) — everything in Starter + unlimited sub-accounts, memberships, API | Max-tier ~$199–$289/mo — 2,500 contacts, 2–3 users, everything in Pro + lead scoring, marketing analytics, promo codes, checkout upsells, 150+ custom fields |
| Top | Agency Pro $497/mo ($4,970/yr) — unlimited sub-accounts, SaaS mode (resell at your own price), white-label desktop, rebilling | Max Classic (custom quote) — the former Infusionsoft flagship, legacy plan for old Infusionsoft accounts |

The pattern to notice: GoHighLevel's three price points are accounts (one business → unlimited sub-accounts → resellable agency). Keap's price points are capacity (contacts + users). Neither has a free plan; both offer 14-day trials.

## The contact-tax math that decides it

This is the section that matters most, so let's run real scenarios. Assume one user, one business, no add-ons.

Scenario A: 2,000 contacts, growing slowly. GoHighLevel Starter: $97/mo + ~$30/mo usage = ~$127/mo real bill, and the list can triple without the bill moving. Keap: a published Pro-tier rate (roughly $129–$229/mo) covers 1,500 contacts — you're already over the base allowance, so contact-tier step-ups apply. At this size the two are roughly comparable; Keap's deeper automation may be worth the premium.

Scenario B: 10,000 contacts. GoHighLevel Starter: still $97/mo + usage (~$127/mo) — the bill doesn't care about your list. Keap: you're several contact tiers past the 1,500–2,500 base allowance, and published guidance puts you in the $200+/mo zone on Pro-tier before extra users. Expect to pay at least 2–3× the GoHighLevel Starter rate for equivalent access — and every 5,000 contacts you add reopens the pricing conversation.

Scenario C: agency, 12 clients. GoHighLevel Agency Pro: $497/mo, unlimited sub-accounts — ~$41/mo per client, plus SaaS mode lets you rebill clients at your own price and keep the margin. Keap: no sub-account model exists — each client needs its own Keap account at full price. Twelve Pro-tier accounts at ~$129–$229/mo each = $1,548–$2,748/mo. This isn't a comparison; it's a category error. Agencies should not be choosing Keap.

The honest framing: Keap's contact tax is fair pricing for what it is — deep automation has a per-record cost, and Infusionsoft always billed this way. But it means Keap gets more expensive the more successful you get, while GoHighLevel's bill is decoupled from your growth. Price your year-one and year-three bills, not the sticker.

## Feature comparison

GoHighLevel gives agencies unlimited sub-accounts, white-label SaaS resale, and unlimited contacts for $97/month flat — Keap offers none of that, one business per account. Keap's counterpunch is the deepest small-business automation: an Infusionsoft-descended campaign builder with lead scoring, plus Keap Pay. Contact math decides it: Keap caps at 1,500–2,500 contacts with paid add-ons (~$29–$30/month each); GoHighLevel charges metered usage instead.

| Capability | GoHighLevel | Keap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CRM + sales pipelines | Yes — pipelines, smart lists, opportunities | Yes — visual pipelines, segmentation, task automation |
| Automation builder depth | Strong workflows across funnels, SMS, email, voice | Deepest in class — Infusionsoft-descended campaign builder, lead scoring, marketing analytics (Max) |
| Email marketing | Yes, with usage-based sending costs | Yes — templates, triggers, A/B testing; 100–150 custom fields |
| SMS / text marketing | Yes — LC phone system, rebillable to clients | Yes — 150–250 included text messages depending on tier |

| Appointments | Yes — calendar, automated reminders | Yes — booking synced with Google Calendar |

Feature availability compiled October 2026 from official documentation and published comparisons. Vendors move features between tiers — confirm on the vendor's site.

## Keap's automation moat

This is where Keap earns its premium, and it's real. The campaign builder is the direct descendant of Infusionsoft's — twenty-plus years of small-business automation DNA, refined into a visual builder that handles branching logic, lead scoring, marketing analytics, promo codes, and checkout upsells (Max tier) that GoHighLevel's workflow builder matches in breadth but not in depth.

Keap Pay is the underrated piece: invoicing, one-click payments, and recurring billing built into the CRM at 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction with no monthly fee. For service businesses and info-product sellers who live in order forms and payment plans, that's one fewer integration to babysit — Stripe bolted onto GoHighLevel works, but it isn't native.

And the small-business ergonomics matter: dedicated phone line on Pro, 100+ custom fields, prebuilt campaign templates loaded with best-practice steps, appointments synced to Google Calendar. Keap is optimized for the solo operator who wants sophisticated automation without a RevOps hire.

## GoHighLevel's counterpunch

GoHighLevel doesn't try to out-automate Keap — it outflanks it. Flat unlimited-contact billing means your bill is decoupled from your growth (see the contact-tax math above). The funnel and website builder plus memberships mean Keap's landing-pages-only approach looks thin. The LC phone/SMS system with rebilling turns communication from a cost center into a margin line for agencies.

But the real counterpunch is SaaS mode: Agency Pro at $497/month lets you resell GoHighLevel itself to clients at whatever price you set, white-labeled. Run 20 clients at $97/month each and the platform pays for itself four times over before you touch a service retainer. Keap has no answer to this — its partner program pays referral-style, not resale-style.

Entry price seals it for the curious: $97/month flat to start , versus Keap's Pro-tier entry at roughly 1.3–2.3× that, contact-limited.

## Who should pick GoHighLevel, and who should pick Keap?

Pick GoHighLevel if you run an agency — sub-accounts and the SaaS model are the whole ballgame — or want flat $97/month billing decoupled from contact count. Pick Keap if you're a small business living inside automation with a modest list, at $129–$229/month. Agencies shouldn't compare: Keap has no agency model.

Pick GoHighLevel if: you run an agency or plan to (sub-accounts + SaaS mode are the whole ballgame); your list is growing fast and you want the bill decoupled from it; you want funnels, websites, phone, and memberships on one invoice; your budget starts at $97/month.

Pick Keap if: you're a single small business with a modest list (under ~5,000 contacts) that lives inside automation — deep branching, lead scoring, upsell funnels, payment plans; you value the deepest campaign builder in the class over the broadest feature set; and you're comfortable with a bill that grows as your list does.

Skip Keap if: you manage client accounts (no sub-accounts — full price per client), your list is already past 10,000 contacts (do the contact-tax math first), or you need real website/funnel building rather than landing pages.

Skip GoHighLevel if: you need the deepest automation branching available and nothing else matters — Keap's campaign builder still wins that fight; or you want a tool with a gentler learning curve (GoHighLevel's 2–4 week ramp is real).

## Frequently asked questions

**Is GoHighLevel cheaper than Keap?**

Yes at the entry tier, and the gap grows with your list. GoHighLevel Starter is $97/month flat with unlimited contacts. Keap's 2026 Pro-tier rates run roughly $129–$229/month by billing cycle and contact tier, with only 1,500–2,500 contacts at the base level. Because Keap bills per contact, its bill climbs while GoHighLevel's stays flat.

**How does Keap's contact-based pricing work?**

Your plan includes a contact allowance — 1,500 contacts on Pro and 2,500 on Max — and the price steps up as your list grows past those tiers. Extra users cost roughly $29–$30/month each, and Keap Pay adds 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction with no monthly fee. There's a 14-day trial and no free plan.

**Can agencies run multiple clients on one Keap account?**

No — Keap has no sub-account model; each client needs its own account at full price. GoHighLevel's Agency Pro ($497/month, $4,970/year) includes unlimited sub-accounts plus SaaS mode for reselling to clients with white-label branding. For agencies managing more than two or three clients, this is the single biggest structural difference.

**What is Keap Max Classic?**

Max Classic is Infusionsoft renamed — Keap's original flagship — still sold on custom-quote pricing for legacy customers. If you're an old Infusionsoft user, you're likely on it; new buyers are generally steered to the current Pro and Max tiers. Expect a sales-led quote process rather than self-serve checkout on Max Classic.

**Which has the better automation builder?**

Keap, for automation depth: its visual campaign builder is the descendant of Infusionsoft's, with lead scoring, marketing analytics, promo codes, and checkout upsells on Max — the deepest branching logic of the two. GoHighLevel's workflow builder is strong and covers the gap in breadth (funnels, websites, LC phone/SMS, memberships, SaaS mode), but pure automation sophistication still belongs to Keap.

**Is GoHighLevel's $97/month really the whole bill?**

No. $97 Starter is the floor, not the ceiling: expect $20–$150/month in usage fees (calls, SMS, email, AI) on top, and the AI Employee add-on is $50/month per sub-account on Starter. Keap has the same problem — the sticker price isn't the whole bill, because contacts grow the bill. Do the year-one math first.

**GoHighLevel vs Keap — which is better?**

For agencies, GoHighLevel — no contest: unlimited sub-accounts, SaaS mode, and white-label resale that Keap simply doesn't have. For a small business that lives inside automation with a modest list, Keap's automation moat can justify its ~$129–$229/mo Pro-tier pricing (1,500 contacts) — as long as the contact tax doesn't bite.

**How much does GoHighLevel really cost per month?**

Starter is $97/mo ($970/yr) with unlimited contacts, Unlimited $297/mo, Agency Pro $497/mo — and then metered usage on top: $20–$150/mo for calls, SMS, email, and AI depending on volume. Budget the usage line item, not just the plan. The plan price alone understates what an agency actually pays each month.

**What happens to my bill as my contact list grows on each?**

This is the deciding math. GoHighLevel: flat unlimited contacts at every tier — the only variable is metered usage ($20–$150/mo for calls, SMS, email, AI). Keap: contact-tier step-ups as your list grows past 1,500 contacts, plus ~$29–$30/mo per extra user. A growing list punishes Keap's pricing and barely touches GoHighLevel's.

**Why do agencies pick GoHighLevel over Keap?**

The agency model: unlimited sub-accounts, SaaS mode that lets you resell the platform at your own price, and white-labeling — none of which Keap has. Add flat unlimited-contact billing and it's not a real contest for agency workflows. Keap's play is the automation moat for small businesses, not agencies.

## Final verdict

Worth it for agencies and growth-stage businesses: GoHighLevel. $97/month flat with unlimited contacts, sub-accounts, SaaS mode, funnels, and a rebillable phone system — the bill is decoupled from your growth, and Agency Pro at $497/month is the cheapest per-client stack in the category. Just budget the real bill ($20–$150/mo usage on top) and the 2–4 week learning curve.

Worth it for automation-first solo businesses: Keap. The deepest campaign builder in the class, native Keap Pay, lead scoring and upsell funnels on Max — if your list is modest and your automation is sophisticated, the contact tax is a fair price for the depth. Just price it at your year-three list size, not today's.

Skip the comparison entirely if you're an agency eyeing Keap — one business per account at full price per client is a non-starter next to unlimited sub-accounts. And skip GoHighLevel if the deepest automation branching is the only thing you care about; Keap still wins that one fight.

### Ready to decide?

Start with the trials: GoHighLevel has a 14-day trial on flat pricing; Keap has a 14-day trial on contact-based pricing. Test with your real list size, not the sticker price.

# GoHighLevel vs Systeme.io: The Honest 2026 Breakdown

Last updated October 2026 · 10 min read · Pricing verified September 2026

In short: Pick systeme.io if you're one person selling courses, coaching, or digital products — start free and pay $0–$17/month while you grow. Pick GoHighLevel if you manage clients, need a real CRM with pipelines and SMS, or want white-label SaaS resale. Solo operators buy systeme.io; agencies buy GoHighLevel. At $97/month each, you're buying opposite things.

GoHighLevel and systeme.io are both sold as "all-in-one" platforms, and both will happily take $97 a month from you. That's roughly where the similarity ends. systeme.io is built for one person running one business: funnels, email, courses, and affiliate management in a dashboard you can learn in an afternoon — with a free plan covering 2,000 contacts. GoHighLevel is built for agencies: a full CRM with pipelines, two-way SMS, sub-accounts for every client, and a SaaS mode that lets you resell the platform itself.

Most comparisons declare a single winner and move on. We won't do that, because these two tools barely compete — they serve different buyers. But there's a trap worth naming: systeme.io's top tier and GoHighLevel's entry tier both cost $97/month, and people absolutely do cross-shop them. Here's the full breakdown, with the pricing math that actually decides it.

A note on how we work: our verdicts come from pricing analysis, documented feature lists, and aggregated verified reviews — not hands-on lab tests. When review sentiment is consistent across sources, we say so; when sources conflict, we say that too.

- systeme.io has a real free plan — 2,000 contacts, 3 funnels, 1 course, unlimited emails, no card required. - Ceiling pricing: systeme.io Unlimited is $97/mo ($80.90/mo annual) with unlimited everything; GoHighLevel Agency Pro is $497/mo (~$414/mo annual) with white-label SaaS resale and up to 10x usage markup. Source: systeme.io official pricing (https://systeme.io/pricing) · Source: GoHighLevel official pricing (https://www.gohighlevel.com/pricing)

## GoHighLevel vs systeme.io at a glance

Solo sellers buy systeme.io; agencies buy GoHighLevel. At $97/month each you're buying opposite things: systeme.io's Unlimited plan ($97/month, $80.90 annual) gives unlimited everything with a free plan (2,000 contacts), while GoHighLevel's Starter ($97/month, ~$81 annual) gives a full CRM with pipelines and SMS. The split: systeme.io is gentle and contact-tiered; GoHighLevel has unlimited contacts but a 2–4 week learning curve.

## Quick questions, quick answers

The questions people ask most about this comparison, answered directly. Stats and pricing verified October 2026.

**GoHighLevel vs systeme.io — which is better for agencies?**

GoHighLevel, by design. Agency Pro is $497/month (~$414 annual) and lets you resell under your own brand with white-label SaaS resale — you can even mark up usage up to 10x. systeme.io has no agency model at all; it's built for solo operators selling courses, coaching, or digital products.

## The quick verdict

Pick systeme.io if you're one person running one business — selling courses, coaching, or digital products — and you want to start free and pay $0–$17/month while you grow. It's the cheapest credible all-in-one in the market.

Pick GoHighLevel if you manage clients, need a real CRM with pipelines and SMS, or want to white-label or resell software as a service. Its sub-account architecture is the product, and nothing at this price does multi-client work better.

The one-sentence version: systeme.io wins on price and simplicity for solo operators; GoHighLevel wins on CRM depth and agency infrastructure. At $97/month each, you're buying opposite things.

Pricing is the whole story here — and the headline numbers hide the real comparison. systeme.io charges per business, with generous free and cheap tiers. GoHighLevel charges per agency seat of power, starting at $97/month with no free plan, then piles usage fees (SMS, calls, AI) on top. Same "$97" figure, opposite philosophies.

## Ease of use

systeme.io's edge — and it's the reason beginners love it. The interface is deliberately simple: one sidebar, one dashboard, no sub-account architecture to understand. Review sentiment is remarkably consistent here — beginners report being up and running in an afternoon, and the platform holds roughly 4.8/5 across G2, Capterra, and Trustpilot in 2026 published comparisons. The trade-off is real, though: that simplicity means fewer knobs when you outgrow the basics.

GoHighLevel is the opposite bet. It's a professional tool with a professional learning curve — reviewers consistently describe a genuinely busy first two to four weeks, with the workflow builder, sub-account setup, and phone/email configuration taking the longest. GHL scores well too (around 4.6/5 on G2 in 2026 roundups, lower on Capterra), but the praise comes overwhelmingly from agencies, and the complaints cluster around complexity and occasional bugginess. If you want "simple," this isn't it — it's "powerful."

## CRM & automation depth

This is GoHighLevel's biggest edge, and it's not close. GHL ships a genuine sales CRM: visual pipelines, opportunity tracking, custom fields, tags, and smart lists — with clean separation between client sub-accounts. Its workflow builder runs multi-channel automations across email, SMS, voice calls, and WhatsApp, with missed-call text-back and review requests baked in. For an agency running follow-up for ten local businesses, this is the product.

systeme.io's automation is rules-based and honest about it: triggers, actions, and conditions, with the rule count scaling by tier (1 on free, 10 on Startup, 100 on Webinar, unlimited on Unlimited). It handles welcome sequences, abandoned carts, and course drips perfectly well. What it doesn't do is pipelines, deal stages, or multi-channel orchestration — there's no SMS at all. If your business lives or dies on sales follow-up, that's a structural gap, not a missing feature you can work around.

## The solo-business math

This is where the decision gets made. Three realistic scenarios, with the numbers:

Scenario A: creator launching a first course. systeme.io Free: $0/year — 2,000 contacts, 3 funnels, 1 course, unlimited emails. That's a complete launch stack for nothing. GoHighLevel Starter: $1,164/year plus usage fees. For a first launch, that's not a comparison — it's a 10x+ cost difference for capacity you won't touch.

Scenario B: coach with 5,000 contacts, email + funnels + one course. systeme.io Startup: $17/month, $204/year. GoHighLevel Starter: $97/month plus ~$20–$50/month in usage, roughly $1,400–$1,800/year. Same job, ~7x the price. Unless you specifically need SMS follow-up or pipeline tracking, the math isn't defensible.

Scenario C: freelancer signing client #3. Now the math flips. systeme.io has no real multi-client architecture — you'd be juggling logins and workarounds. GoHighLevel Unlimited at $297/month gives every client an isolated sub-account, white-labeled, with usage rebilled to their cards. At three clients paying you even modest retainers, the platform cost per client drops under $100/month — and it replaces a stack (funnels + email tool + Calendly + SMS + reputation management) that 2026 reviews consistently price at $400–$600/month separately.

The honest upgrade path: start on systeme.io free, grow into the $17 Startup plan, and switch to GoHighLevel when client revenue covers the $97–$297/month. They're complements across a business lifecycle, not pure rivals. systeme.io's Unlimited plan even advertises free migration assistance — the vendors know this path exists.

## Who should pick GoHighLevel, and who should pick Systeme.io?

Pick systeme.io if you're one person selling courses, coaching, or digital products — start free, pay $0–$17/month while growing. Pick GoHighLevel if you manage clients, need a real CRM with pipelines and SMS, or want white-label SaaS resale at $97/month. Solo operators buy systeme.io; agencies buy GoHighLevel.

- You're one person running one business

- You sell courses, coaching, or digital products

- You want to start free and keep costs under ~$50/mo

- Webinars or affiliate management matter to you

- You want to be live this week, not next month

### Pick GoHighLevel if…

- You manage 2+ clients (or plan to)

- You're replacing a $400+/mo stack of separate tools
